newsitem.title: MEXICO: Eight unions bolt from top Mexican labor congress.
newsitem.headline: Eight unions bolt from top Mexican labor congress.

text.p: Mexico's largest labor congress suffered an unprecedented setback on Wednesday when eight leading unions decided to abandon the group.

The dissidents said on Thursday they were fed up with the undemocratic ways of the Labor Congress, or Congreso de Trabajo (CT) in Spanish, and would form a rival group that could include more than 100 additional unions.

"The (CT) has not responded to the demands of the workers," Alejandra Barrales, leader of the coalition that bolted, told Reuters. "We gave them three years to try to revive the organization and no longer subordinate themselves to the interests of the government and the bosses."
Founded in 1966, the CT is Mexico's largest labor umbrella group, encompassing 42 unions and 10 million workers, about one-ninth of the country's population.
It is a major player in formulating the government's annual economic policy in the so-called "Pacto" alliance of business, labor and government.
The pro-goverment group is known more for promoting stability than militant activism on behalf of workers.

Barrales, leader of a union group known as FESEBES, likened the breakaways to the recent elections in Mexico, in which opposition parties scored historic victories against the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), which has ruled Mexico for 68 years.
"It's part of the process of Mexicans truly participating in ... the democratization of the country," she said.

The eight unions who left represent 750,000 workers, Barrales said. She added another 26 unions have agreed to join the breakaway group which will hold a general assembly August 22-23, while 76 more independent unions are considering the new alliance.
By abandoning the CT at Wednesday's extraordinary assembly, the dissidents thwarted plans to name a new president by consensus.
Instead, an open CT election to replace outgoing president Victor Flores Morales was set for August 20.
"They (the eight unions) were within their rights to leave, but I don't think this was the best timing," CT Vice President Enrique Aguilar Borrego told Reuters in an interview on Thursday.

"I think now more than ever the congress is showing signs of change," Aguilar Borrego, a candidate for CT president, added in defense of the CT. "I'm not saying it's a profound change, but it is some change."

The CT had taken on a higher profile since the death in June of 97-year-old Fidel Velazquez, the powerful leader of the Confederation of Mexican Workers (CTM). Technically, the CTM came under the aegis of the CT, but it wielded more clout because of Velazquez, a confidante to presidents over the past six decades.

Barrales said the eight breakaway unions are telephone workers (STRM), transportation workers (ATM), technical workers (STYM), electricicans (SME), flight attendants (ASSA) and pilots (ASPA), social security workers (SNTSS), and nuclear industry workers (SUFIN).
